After the Soviet invasion of Afghanistan in 1979, millions of Afghans fled across the border into Pakistan, mostly to the province now called Khyber Pakhtunkhwa and to Balochistan. By the late 1980s more than three million lived there, the largest refugee population in the world at the time.

Most were Pashtuns, who share language and kin with people on the Pakistani side. Camps around Peshawar became bases for the mujahideen fighting the Soviets, armed through Pakistan with American and Saudi money. Religious schools in the camps later produced many members of the Taliban.

Many went home after the Soviets left in 1989, but new wars kept sending people back, and a generation grew up in Pakistan knowing no other home. Pakistan's welcome cooled over the decades, and from 2023 it began deporting Afghans without papers. The same flight sent millions to Iran; see Afghan refugees in Iran and the wider Afghan refugee exodus.
